title: William James
summary: William James was an American philosopher and psychologist and one of the founders of pragmatism. He believed ideas should be tested by the difference they make in life, and he was one of the first to describe consciousness as a living, continuous “stream.” Having gone through a severe emotional crisis in his youth, he wrote about inner life with rare compassion.
onEmotions: James proposed a famous theory, known as the James–Lange theory: an emotion is, to a large extent, the feeling of bodily changes. We don't simply cry because we are sad: the sensation of tears, breathing and tension is itself a large part of sadness. Hence a practical conclusion: through the body, attention and action we can influence our feelings. James also wrote a great deal about habit, about belief, and about the “sick soul” — people who feel the dark side of life keenly — and considered their experience no less valuable than that of natural optimists.

anxiety.text: James would ask not “what are you anxious about?” but “where is your anxiety right now — in your chest, your throat, your shoulders?” It's a hard state, and he, who went through attacks of fear in his youth, knew it from the inside. His theory of emotions points to something important: anxiety lives largely in the body — a racing heart, uneven breathing, tense muscles. This doesn't mean it isn't “real.” But it does mean the body is not only the place where anxiety is felt, but also a door through which it can be influenced. In his essay “The Gospel of Relaxation,” James advised acting and speaking “as if” the state you want were already there. So you can start by breathing and moving more calmly. Anxiety won't vanish on command, but its bodily basis can loosen a little — and the feeling itself grows quieter.
anxiety.practice: Find where exactly the anxiety sits and put your palm there. Take five exhales, each a little longer than the inhale — acting “as if” the calm had already come, as James advised.

fear.text: We see a bear and run — and only then, according to James, are we afraid, because we run. If you're frightened right now, there is unexpected support in this paradox. In his theory of emotions James put forward an unusual idea. We usually think that first we get scared and then we tremble. He believed the opposite: the body reacts first — the heart pounds, the muscles tense — and fear is to a large extent the feeling of these changes. This doesn't make fear a mistake: the body instantly assesses danger and prepares us for it. But it helps us deal with it. Fear is not a verdict that you are a coward but a wave of bodily reaction with a beginning and an end. You can notice it, name it and wait it out without merging with it: “my body is preparing for danger right now.”
fear.practice: Say to yourself: “My body is getting ready to run from a bear.” Notice three bodily sensations — heart, breath, muscles — and watch how the wave changes, without running from it.

quote.text: We feel sorry because we cry, angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. XXV “The Emotions” (1890)

sadness.text: James divided people into the “healthy-minded” — natural optimists — and “sick souls,” who keenly feel the sorrowful side of life, and he considered the latter's experience fuller, because it takes in everything there is in the world, including pain. If you're sad right now, perhaps this is how you are seeing — more broadly and honestly, not worse than others. Such sadness doesn't need to be hurried or hidden. Your sadness is not an error of perception but a way of seeing reality more deeply. James wrote that such people, having passed through darkness, often arrive at a more lasting joy — he called them the “twice-born.” Sadness can be part of that path rather than a dead end.
sadness.practice: Walk slowly for ten minutes without trying to cheer yourself up — just let the sadness walk beside you. The “sick soul,” for James, sees more: notice what you in particular see today.

grief.text: James's farewell letter to his dying father arrived too late; his brother Henry read it aloud at the grave. Grief can't be fixed with advice. His theory of emotions shows how closely feelings are tied to the body: grief is felt as heaviness in the chest, a lump in the throat, tiredness — and this is a living organism's natural response to loss. In The Principles of Psychology he wrote that the people close to us become part of our “self,” and when they go, a part of us goes with them. No wonder grief also feels like a loss of oneself. From a pragmatic point of view, small everyday actions can be something to lean on: they help life go on while the feeling is lived through at its own pace.
grief.practice: Say aloud a few words addressed to the person you lost — by a window or a photograph, the way Henry read his brother's letter at the grave. Then do one small kind thing for your body: a glass of water, a warm blanket, a short walk.

loneliness.text: Hardly any punishment more cruel could be devised, James wrote, than to be turned loose in society and remain absolutely unnoticed. If you're lonely right now, that line explains why it hurts so much. In The Principles of Psychology he described the “social self” — the part of our self that lives in the recognition of others. He wrote that a person has as many social selves as there are individuals who recognize them and carry an image of them in their minds. Loneliness is not a whim but the hunger of a very important part of you. This helps you accept the feeling without shame. James's pragmatism also suggests a direction: look not at all your connections at once, but at what small step toward someone is possible today.
loneliness.practice: Give one person a sign today that you've noticed them: call the shop assistant by name, ask a neighbour how they are, answer a friend with your voice instead of an emoji. The “social self,” for James, grows in both directions.

anger.text: “Refuse to express a passion, and it dies”: this line of James's sounds harsh, but behind it lies simple bodily mechanics. Anger is a strong feeling, and there is often truth in it: something has touched your boundaries. Starting from his theory of emotions, James noticed that the bodily expression of a feeling largely feeds it. In The Principles of Psychology he wrote that if you count ten before venting your anger, its occasion may come to seem quite different. There is a space between the flare-up and the action. It isn't about pretending there is no anger — James, in fact, showed that feelings are real and bodily. It's about letting the body calm down a little and then calmly deciding what you want to do about what made you angry. Anger then becomes information rather than a command.
anger.practice: When anger rises, step out for a couple of minutes and walk slowly, counting your steps to ten: the body calms down faster than thoughts. Then ask: what exactly touched me, and what do I want to do about it?

shame.text: James told of a man mortally ashamed of being only the second-best boxer in the world, though he yields to just one person. If you feel ashamed right now, that absurd story may be more about you than it seems. James proposed a simple but deep formula: self-esteem equals our successes divided by our pretensions. That is, we suffer not simply from failures but from the gap between what we have achieved and what we expected of ourselves. Shame can be reduced not only by increasing the “numerator” — successes — but also by revisiting the “denominator”: the demands you have taken on. James wrote that to give up some pretensions is as blessed a relief as to have them gratified.
shame.practice: Read James's words aloud: “To give up pretensions is as blessed a relief as to get them gratified.” Name one demand on yourself that you could give up today, even halfway.

quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. X “The Consciousness of Self” (1890)

guilt.text: “Seize the very first possible opportunity to act on every resolution you make,” James advised in his chapter on habit. Guilt is heavy, and it often shows that acting well matters to you. As a pragmatist, James looked at ideas and feelings with a question: what difference does this make in life? So guilt is useful when it leads to action — an apology, a repair, a new habit — and becomes barren when it just goes round in circles. James valued habit highly: he wrote that our character is largely built out of many small repeated actions. So making amends doesn't require instantly turning into a different person: it's enough to take a first step and repeat it.
guilt.practice: Take one small step toward repair today — a message of apology, a returned item, a phone call — while the resolution is still warm. For James, the first opportunity is the most important one.

envy.text: Handsome, athletic, rich, witty, a lady-killer, a philosopher and a saint — James admitted he'd like to be all of these, but “the philosopher and the lady-killer could not well keep house in the same tenement of clay.” When envy stings, that honest smile is worth remembering. In The Principles of Psychology James described a person's self very broadly: it includes not only the body and thoughts but also clothes, home, family, work, reputation. Everything we call “mine” becomes part of us. Envy is when someone else's “mine” touches ours: as if another person has a piece of the self we would like to have. James also noted that no one can be everything at once. Having chosen one self, you have to give up the others. Envy can remind you of your choice and its value.
envy.practice: Imagine living the whole life of the person you envy — morning to night, with all its renunciations. Which of your own selves would you have to give up in exchange? Would you want that trade?

emptiness.text: On April 30, 1870, the twenty-eight-year-old James, who had lived in apathy for months, wrote in his diary: “My first act of free will shall be to believe in free will.” If you feel empty and drained right now, know that he started from the same place. Sometimes you don't need to wait for meaning to appear before you begin to act: a small action can itself become the beginning of meaning. This echoes his idea of “the will to believe”: in some matters our belief and our steps help create what we believe in. James promised no quick solutions, but he showed that even a tiny choice brings back the sense of taking part in your own life.
emptiness.practice: Choose one very small action for the next hour — make the bed, open a window, water a plant — and do it simply because you decided to. That's your “first act of free will” for today.

quote.text: My first act of free will shall be to believe in free will.
quote.author: William James

confusion.text: A baby, James wrote, experiences the world as “one great blooming, buzzing confusion.” When thoughts and feelings get tangled and there's no clear answer, we briefly return to that cradle, and there's nothing shameful in it. James described consciousness as a “stream”: it isn't made of neat separate pieces but flows continuously, sometimes in quick “flights,” sometimes in slow “perchings.” In this stream there is always a “fringe” — vague sensations, half-thoughts, premonitions we can't yet name. Confusion is not a malfunction but a moment when the stream has a lot of fringe and few clear resting places. This is an ordinary part of how the mind works. James's pragmatism adds a piece of advice: if it's unclear which thought is right, ask what practical difference each option would make. Clarity often comes not in the head but in action.
confusion.practice: Put pragmatism's main question to your confusion: “What practical difference would it make?” Take two thoughts you're torn between and imagine what you'd do tomorrow if each were true. If nothing changes, the argument can be let go.

fatigue.text: “Unclamp your intellectual and practical machinery,” James urged in “The Gospel of Relaxation” (1899), looking at people who hurry and tense their muscles, faces and voices even when there's no need. If you're worn out, it's an honest signal: your strength has become less than what's demanded of you. According to his theory of emotions, such bodily tension itself feeds the feeling of anxiety and exhaustion. Burnout is not only a lot of work but also a habit of always being keyed up. James advised learning to let tension go: relaxing the body, not wasting energy on needless hurry, allowing yourself pauses. This isn't laziness but sensible care for a resource that isn't infinite.
fatigue.practice: Unclench, one by one, whatever is tight for no reason: forehead, jaw, shoulders, fists. With each exhale, silently say James's word: “Unclamp.”

boredom.text: James spent a week at the model resort of Chautauqua — lectures, cleanliness, perfect order — and on leaving exclaimed, “Ouf! what a relief!” Boredom can arise even where everything is in order: the world goes flat, and it's unpleasant. He showed that habit saves energy: repeated actions become automatic, and we stop noticing them. This is useful, but there is a flip side — life can turn into a background we don't look at. Boredom is not necessarily a “boring world” but attention sliding over the familiar. James also noted that interest is born from connecting something new with what we already care about. So boredom can be met with curiosity: find one unnoticed detail in the familiar and connect it with what matters to you.
boredom.practice: Walk a familiar route and find three details on it you had never noticed. For each one ask, as James taught: what that matters to me is it connected with?

quote.text: My experience is what I agree to attend to.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. XI “Attention” (1890)

joy.text: James loved Stevenson's story of boys who hid tin lanterns under their coats and were happy simply because the lanterns were burning there. Your joy, like such a lantern, needs no explaining to anyone — you can simply let it burn. Studying emotions, James showed how joy takes hold of the whole body: lightness, squared shoulders, a smile, the urge to move. For him these are not secondary “expressions” but the very fabric of the feeling. Joy doesn't only come to us — we can support it a little through the body: notice the smile, not hurry to hide it, let it last. In The Varieties of Religious Experience, James described with interest people of a “healthy-minded” outlook, who know how to notice the good and give themselves to it. In his view, this can partly be learned — through attention and a habit of noticing.
joy.practice: Stay in the joy for three breaths, like a boy with a lantern under his coat: where is it burning in your body? Show it to no one — just let it flare up a little.

love.text: The self, for James, doesn't end at the skin: it includes your home, your clothes, your work — and the people you love. The tenderness you feel right now is the sense of that boundary widening to let someone else in. From the standpoint of his theory of emotions, tenderness is a whole complex of sensations: warmth in the chest, softness in the face, the wish to touch. It is not an illusion but a living response of the whole organism. In The Principles of Psychology James also wrote that the people we love become part of our extended self: we experience their joys and troubles almost as our own. This makes us more vulnerable, but also richer. Pragmatism would add: love reveals itself in the difference it makes — in words, care, small acts.
love.practice: Tell the person you love one specific thing you notice in them — not “I love you” but “I like the way you…”. Pragmatism tests love by the difference it makes.

gratitude.text: “My experience is what I agree to attend to,” James wrote. When gratitude warms you, you are choosing what gets into your experience. James would add three things. First, emotion lives in the body: gratitude is warmth, relaxation, sometimes tears, and it's worth not skipping past it but feeling it through. Second, our experience is made of what we pay attention to: if you notice the good, the world really does become different for you. Third, James believed habits are formed by repetition. Gratitude, too, can become a habit — not out of duty, but because the mind gradually learns to see what supports you. This doesn't cancel difficulties, but it adds to the picture what is already there.
gratitude.practice: Say “thank you” to one person for something specific they did today or recently — out loud or in a message. That's how gratitude slowly turns from a feeling into a habit.

hope.text: A climber stands before a chasm, and the only way on is a leap: James wrote that confidence in success itself helps make it. If you're hoping for something, you're standing at your own chasm. In his essay “The Will to Believe” he argued that in some matters we have the right to believe even without conclusive evidence — especially when the belief itself affects the outcome. Hope is not self-deception but taking part in creating the future: it gives you strength to act, and actions change reality. Hope doesn't guarantee an outcome. But it makes the step possible — and James believed that it is in this step that our freedom shows itself.
hope.practice: Stand as if before a leap: feet steady, shoulders open, leaning slightly forward. Name your first small step out loud — and feel your body getting ready for it.

quote.text: Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: “Is Life Worth Living?” (1895), in The Will to Believe (1897)

nostalgia.text: Why do I recognize yesterday's memory as mine and not as someone else's story? James answered: our own experiences come back with a particular “warmth and intimacy.” If the past is tugging at you right now, that is the warmth you feel. Nostalgia is the feeling of that very warmth, a sense of the continuity of your self. The stream of consciousness flows, everything changes, and yet you remain yourself — the past is felt as your own. Nostalgia then is not only longing for what is lost but also confirmation that your life is one story. And this warmth can be carried into the present, not only sought behind you.
nostalgia.practice: Carry one thread of that warmth into today: brew that same tea, play that song, call that person. The stream flows on, but the self in it is one.

craving.text: James described how two ideas struggle in consciousness: one pulls toward a familiar pleasure, the other toward what you want for yourself as a whole. A sharp craving can be almost physical, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. He considered attention decisive: will, for James, is largely the effort of holding the right thought before your mind until the wave subsides. And in The Varieties of Religious Experience he soberly noted that the pull toward intoxication often hides a thirst for something greater — expansion, union, a “yes” to the world — which intoxication itself fulfills only briefly and at a high price. A craving is not a verdict but a wave and a question: what am I really looking for?
craving.practice: When the craving comes, name it out loud: “This is a wave.” Hold one thought about what matters to you before your mind and keep breathing until the wave begins to subside — that, for James, is will.

addiction.text: In an old play, Rip Van Winkle excused every lapse with “I won't count this time” — but James noted that the nervous system counts everything. And it counts every step in the other direction just as faithfully. In his chapter on habit he described the nervous system as a plastic material: a repeated action wears an ever-deeper groove, and following it becomes almost automatic. This explains why it is so hard to break the cycle, and it lifts the charge of “weak will.” But the same thought gives rise to hope: plasticity works both ways, and a new groove is also worn by repetition. James advised relying on support from outside and on every small action in the right direction. And in The Varieties of Religious Experience he described with respect people who found a way out through community and a change in what they leaned on inside.
addiction.practice: Notice today one small action toward a new groove and tell yourself: “This counts.” If you like, think about who could support you — someone close, or a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: “What difference does it make?” — pragmatism's main question fits the morning after: how much of this gloom is the truth about your life, and how much the voice of a worn-out body? Your body aches, anxiety and shame pile on, and there's no need to punish yourself. James reminds us that emotions are largely born from bodily sensations. When the body is dehydrated, worn out and overstimulated, it produces anxiety and gloom all by itself — and the mind readily finds explanations for them: “I've ruined everything,” “everyone is judging me.” Much of the morning anxiety is the voice of the body, not an accurate assessment of your life. This doesn't mean last night doesn't matter. But big conclusions about yourself are better postponed until your body has recovered.
hangover.practice: Drink some water, exhale slowly and sort it out loud: “This is my body. Conclusions about life can wait until tomorrow.” James would call it testing ideas with a clear head.

euphoria.text: James was a pragmatist even in rapture: of any strong experience he asked what fruits it bears. If the world seems to have flung itself open right now, there's no need to spoil it with suspicion — better to think about the harvest. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he described states in which everything seems connected, important, possible — and he believed they have a value of their own: they show that ordinary everyday consciousness is only one form of experience. You can not only live through euphoria but also “gather the harvest”: notice what thoughts and desires it opens up, and what of this is worth taking into ordinary days. The high will pass, but what you found can stay.
euphoria.practice: Gather the harvest: write down one thought or desire from this high. In a couple of days, reread it and ask, in James's manner: what difference could this make in my life?

crash.text: “Sit all day in a moping posture, sigh, and reply to everything with a dismal voice, and your melancholy lingers,” James wrote. The drop after a high is unpleasant and often frightening: it seems the grayness is now forever. According to his theory of emotions, a feeling is largely the sensation of a bodily state. After a strong high — a celebration, a success, a sleepless night — the body is depleted, and its tiredness is experienced as gloom and meaninglessness. The comedown is not a revelation that life is empty but a natural swing that will pass as you recover. James also described consciousness as a “stream”: states in it don't stand still, one flows into another. The drop is part of the stream too. You don't have to believe everything it whispers.
crash.practice: Do the opposite of the “moping posture”: stand up, open your shoulders, walk around the room and say in an ordinary voice: “This is a comedown, not the truth about my life.”

panic.text: “A French correspondent” — that's how James signed, in The Varieties of Religious Experience, the story of his own terror: one evening at dusk he suddenly recalled an asylum patient and felt a “fear of my own existence.” If your heart is pounding and it seems something terrible is about to happen, you're in the company of someone who lived through it. He lived through it and went on living and working. His theory of emotions says: fear is largely the sensation of a racing heart, broken breathing, tension. That means fear can also be influenced through the body. Such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You don't need to defeat it now — you need to help your body pass through it: an exhale, something solid underfoot, attention to what's around you.
panic.practice: Put your feet on the floor and give your body the posture of a calm person: lower your shoulders, unclench your hands. Several times, breathe out more slowly than you breathe in, and silently name five objects you can see.

dread.text: “Be not afraid of life. Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact” — that is how James ended his lecture “Is Life Worth Living?” If the question “what's the point of it all?” is closing over you, he would treat it with enormous respect. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he distinguished the “healthy-minded,” who don't notice the dark side of life, from the “sick soul,” who sees it keenly. And he believed the latter sees more, not less. He himself went through a severe crisis. His pragmatic answer was not consolation in words: in the lecture “Is Life Worth Living?” he said that meaning does not lie ready-made but is partly created by our participation — belief, action, care. Dread can be acknowledged as an honest question, answered not by reasoning but by the steps of life.
dread.practice: Read aloud slowly: “Believe that life is worth living, and your belief will help create the fact.” Then do one small task in which you are needed today — even just a little.

fomo.text: As a young man James studied painting and seriously meant to become an artist — and became a doctor, a psychologist, a philosopher instead. The feeling that everyone else lives more interesting lives while you miss the main thing is exhausting; James knew the price of every closed door. In The Principles of Psychology he wrote that each of us has many possible selves: you could become a scientist, a traveler, the life of the party — but you can't become all of them at once. Choosing one means giving up the others, and this is not a defeat but a condition of life. James even said that giving up pretensions brings relief. The fear of missing out is the inevitable shadow of any choice. It doesn't mean you chose wrongly. It means you are a living person in a world where there are more possibilities than lives.
fomo.practice: Sit for five minutes wherever you are, without your phone, and quietly tell the possibilities you're missing right now: “This isn't mine for now.” Notice how your body responds to the self you have chosen.

sleepless.text: James compared consciousness to a bird's flight: “flights” alternate with “perchings,” and no command will make it settle on a branch. At three in the morning, when sleep won't come, that flight is especially noisy, and fighting it by force rarely works. James described consciousness as a “stream”: thoughts flow by themselves, one catching on another, and they can't be stopped on command. At night, with no outside tasks, this stream becomes especially loud, and the body, according to James's theory of emotions, adds its own tension, which itself colors thoughts with anxiety. In “The Gospel of Relaxation” James advised not fighting the state but letting go of muscular tension and hurry. Nighttime thoughts are not necessarily true: at three in the morning everything looks darker than it is. You can let the stream flow without following every thought.
sleepless.practice: Lying down, picture your thoughts as birds flitting from branch to branch — don't chase them away. Meanwhile move your attention up through your body and with each exhale release one place: feet, belly, shoulders, jaw, forehead.

betrayal.text: A handful of highwaymen can rob a whole train because each passenger fears to trust the others — James gives this example in “The Will to Believe.” When your trust has been betrayed, what you leaned on collapses, and this pain is legitimate. James wrote a lot about trust as a practical force: in his essay “The Will to Believe” he noted that many human bonds rest on someone being willing to trust first — and without that willingness no cooperation is possible. Betrayal shows the other side: trust is always a risk. Your pain doesn't prove you were naive. You were doing what makes life among people possible at all. James would add: the question is not whether to trust at all, but whom and how much. That can be decided gradually, drawing on experience rather than fear.
betrayal.practice: Say out loud — to yourself or to someone nearby: “I trusted because…” James would call it not a mistake but the courage of the passenger who dared to go first.

jealousy.text: Each of us, James thought, carries our self in the eyes of those who love us — so when that gaze turns elsewhere, part of you seems to go with it. That burning mix of fear, hurt and insecurity is familiar to almost everyone. In The Principles of Psychology James counted jealousy among the very ancient, instinctive reactions shared by humans and animals. This helps you not to be ashamed of the feeling itself: it arises faster than we can think. When it seems that recognition is going to someone else, our very self-esteem suffers. So jealousy is less about the other person than about the fear of losing your place in someone's life. You can acknowledge this feeling without immediately turning it into action: the wave rises and falls.
jealousy.practice: Notice where you feel jealousy in your body. Tell yourself: “I'm afraid of losing my place in someone's gaze.” Breathe with this for a minute without doing anything.

resentment.text: What does the one who hurt you see when they remember that day? James would probably answer: almost nothing. A long-held grudge is a heavy load, and almost always a real injustice stands behind it. In his essay “On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings” he wrote that we are almost always blind to the inner lives of others: we don't see what matters to them, what torments them, what they live for. This blindness is mutual. The person who hurt you most likely didn't see your pain — and perhaps still doesn't. Resentment often rests on waiting for the other person to finally understand. That waiting is understandable, but it ties you to them. Sometimes relief comes when you acknowledge your own truth yourself, without waiting for them to acknowledge it.
resentment.practice: Write a letter you don't need to send: “It hurt me because…” End with the sentence: “I acknowledge this myself — without waiting for you to see it.”

heartbreak.text: “All that a man can call his” — that is how broadly James defined the self: body, home, plans, loved ones. If it hurts so much right now that it's hard to breathe, this definition is the explanation: a piece has been taken out of your self, and it needs time. When someone close leaves, we lose part of our own extended self, and that is why the pain feels almost physical. This is no exaggeration. The grief of a breakup is the work of rebuilding yourself: an important part has been taken out of your self, and it takes time to find a new balance. James the pragmatist would add that the habits that connected you to the person will keep echoing for a long time. Gradually, new ones will take their place.
heartbreak.practice: Pick the hour that reminds you of the person most painfully and put a tiny new ritual there, just for yourself: a different cup, a different route, one song. New grooves are worn by repetition.

impostor.text: Having finished The Principles of Psychology after twelve years, James called it “a loathsome, distended, tumefied, bloated, dropsical mass” proving only that “W.J. is an incapable.” If you fear being found out, you're in the company of the author of a classic. James proposed a useful formula: self-esteem depends on the ratio of successes to pretensions. The higher we set the bar, the less any real result pleases us. Impostor syndrome often grows out of inflated pretensions: it seems that a “real expert” knows everything, while you only know a lot. James wrote that we have many “social selves” — we are different for different people — and this is not deception but simply how a human being is made. He also noted that giving up unbearable pretensions brings almost as much relief as fulfilling them. You can allow yourself not to be perfect — and still remain yourself.
impostor.practice: Read aloud James's verdict on his own book — “a loathsome, distended, tumefied, bloated, dropsical mass” — and smile: that book became a classic. Then name one demand on yourself you can honestly cross out.

quote.text: To give up pretensions is as blessed a relief as to get them gratified.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. X “The Consciousness of Self” (1890)

self_hatred.text: The inner judge, James might say, is not the voice of truth but a habit, a groove the thought runs along because it has run there a thousand times. When that voice insists you're bad and worthless, it hurts badly — and it's wrong, however convincing it sounds. James himself went through a severe crisis and long self-criticism in his youth. His way out was not to out-argue the inner judge but a practical step: he decided to believe in his own free will and to act without waiting for the doubts to disappear. James also showed that self-esteem depends on our pretensions: if our demands on ourselves are inflated, anyone will seem a failure to themselves. So the critic is a consequence of a bar that can be reconsidered. You don't need to love yourself first in order to take a step.
self_hatred.practice: Imagine a close friend speaking about themselves this way, and say out loud what you would answer. Then repeat the same words to yourself: a new groove begins with the first time.

helplessness.text: In any situation, James the pragmatist would ask not “can I change everything?” but “what difference can my next step make?” Helplessness is heavy: it seems nothing can be changed, and that sense often reflects real limits. James, who went through a crisis of powerlessness in his youth, came to a pragmatic conclusion: we can't know in advance whether our efforts will be enough, but some things become possible only when we act as if they were possible. In “The Will to Believe” he wrote that there are cases where faith in a result itself helps bring it about. This is not “think positive” and not a promise that everything will work out. It's an invitation to find a small area where your step changes something, and to lean on it. Then helplessness is not the end but the place where a very small action begins.
helplessness.practice: Find an action that takes less than five minutes and touches the situation even slightly: a call, a question, an object moved. Do it and notice what difference it made — if only in how you feel.

procrastination.text: A cold morning, an unheated room, and you lie there knowing it's time to get up — that's how James opens his analysis of the will, with humor and sympathy. If you can't get started, it isn't laziness but a state everyone knows. And suddenly, at a moment when you've been distracted from the struggle, you're already on your feet. James believed that action begins when the right thought occupies consciousness without interference — not when we force ourselves. So procrastination doesn't need to be defeated with moral reproaches. What helps is making the needed thought simple and near: not “write the report” but “open the file.” Everything else may begin on its own.
procrastination.practice: Phrase your first step so that it takes less than a minute — “open the document,” “get out my trainers.” Think only about it, as on that cold morning — and suddenly you'll find yourself on your feet.

uprooted.text: James grew up between continents: his father took the children through Geneva, Paris, London and Bonn, and every new school meant starting over. When a move takes away the ground under your feet, the familiar language and the rhythm of life, that is a real loss. According to his theory, a huge part of our life rests on habits: they save energy and give a sense of stability. When you move, hundreds of habits break at once, and everything that used to happen by itself now requires effort. Hence the exhausting tiredness and disorientation. James also wrote about the “social self”: we live in the recognition of people who know us, and in a new place no one knows us yet. Your heaviness is the natural price of rebuilding. New habits and connections form gradually, one repetition at a time.
uprooted.practice: Start one small daily habit in the new place — the same walk, the same café. Notice how it becomes “yours.”

overload.text: “The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook,” wrote James, one of the first to study attention. When the flood of information tears your attention to pieces, it isn't your inability to concentrate: that's how the flood itself works. He wrote that attention is choice: we perceive the world only by selecting a small part of it, and it is this selection that makes experience ours. When the flow is too great, choice becomes impossible, and consciousness is swamped. Overload is not a personal failure but a signal that your choice has been taken away. You can get it back through small decisions: what I'm not reading now, what I'm not answering, what I'm leaving without attention.
overload.practice: Choose three things you can consciously skip today, and for five minutes close every window and tab. Sit in silence, repeating: “I'm not taking this on.”

quote.text: The art of being wise is the art of knowing what to overlook.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. XXII “Reasoning” (1890)

unreality.text: “The Perception of Reality” — James gave a whole chapter of the Principles this title, showing that the feeling “this is real” isn't self-evident and can weaken. If the world or you yourself feel unreal right now, it's strange and unsettling; treat yourself gently. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he cited accounts of people for whom the world suddenly became distant, alien, as if behind glass, and he treated them without judgment. From James's point of view, the sense of reality is closely tied to the body and to a living interest in things. So you can return to it through sensations and simple action, without arguing with yourself.
unreality.practice: Touch a nearby surface with your palm — a table, a wall, fabric. Name three sensations out loud: temperature, texture, pressure. For James, the sense of reality begins in the body.

awe.text: One summer night in 1898 James wandered the moonlit Adirondack woods and later wrote to his wife that the gods of all the nature-mythologies seemed to be meeting in his breast. Awe like that is rare and precious, and James studied it seriously. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he described states in which a person feels connected with something greater than themselves, and he identified their features: they are hard to put into words, and at the same time they feel like knowledge, like revelation. James was in no hurry to explain such experiences as “merely” physiology: he believed they should be judged by their fruits — by how they change a life. Your awe is not an empty emotion but a moment when the familiar frame widens. You can simply live it and remember it.
awe.practice: Stay silently for one more minute with whatever filled you with awe. Then try to find one word for it — and notice, as James once did, that words fall short.

quote.text: Our normal waking consciousness, rational consciousness as we call it, is but one special type of consciousness, whilst all about it, parted from it by the filmiest of screens, there lie potential forms of consciousness entirely different.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Varieties of Religious Experience, Lectures XVI–XVII “Mysticism” (1902)

relief.text: What difference is this relief making in your body right now? That's where James would begin. Something has let go, you can breathe out — allow yourself to feel it fully. By his theory of emotions, James would say that relief is largely the sensation of the body unclenching: the shoulders relax, breathing deepens. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he also described deeper moments of relief — when a person stops holding everything up alone and feels they can trust, let go. James considered such experiences very important: they show how much energy we usually spend on tension. Relief is a hint: this is what your body can be like without the extra load. It's worth noticing and remembering.
relief.practice: Notice where in your body things have become lighter right now. Rest your palm there for a few breaths and simply stay with the sensation.

calm.text: James delivered his “Gospel of Relaxation” to graduates of a Boston gymnastics school and urged them not to live in constant hurry and tension when there's no need. The calm you feel right now is a precious state, and it needs no justification. According to his theory of emotions, bodily tension itself generates anxiety, and relaxation generates calm. Calm is not laziness or inaction but a resource from which clear and strong activity is later born. James believed that calm composure works better than convulsive effort. So you can not only value your calm but also memorize it with your body, to make it easier to return to later.
calm.practice: Memorize how your shoulders, face and breathing feel right now. Come up with a short anchor word for this state, so your body can find its way back later.

inspiration.text: In “The Energies of Men” (1907) James described “second wind”: after the first tiredness a new layer of strength suddenly opens, while usually we live on only a small part of our capacities, unaware of the reserves. If your strength seems to be flowing in right now and you want to make, invent, create, this vivid, living state is worth protecting. Inspiration is a moment when we touch these reserves. James didn't consider this mysticism: such powers are unlocked by strong ideas, enthusiasm, the example of other people. Inspiration shouldn't be spent on worrying about where it will go. Better to give it a task — even a small one — so that the energy you've found has time to become an act.
inspiration.practice: Give the energy you've found a task right now: one first step toward the idea — a sketch, a call, an open page. James believed second wind opens up in action, not in waiting.

quote.text: Compared with what we ought to be, we are only half awake.
quote.author: William James

schadenfreude.text: James admitted that, having staked his all on psychology, he was mortified if others knew more of it than he did, yet perfectly content to be ignorant of Greek. That small glee at someone else's failure is unpleasant to notice, but it's very human and says nothing final about you. He showed that our self-esteem is largely built on comparison. His formula “self-esteem equals success divided by pretensions” also explains schadenfreude: someone else's failure seems for a moment to narrow the gap between us and who we would like to be. Schadenfreude is a signal not of malice but of wounded self-esteem looking for a breather. James believed it's useful to treat feelings as facts of experience: notice them, name them, ask where they lead. Then schadenfreude becomes a hint — about where comparing yourself hurts.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “Where have I staked my all, if I'm comparing myself with this person?” Name one pretension that could be loosened a little — the way James calmly didn't know Greek.

contempt.text: Driving through the mountains of North Carolina, James saw only ugly clearings around him — until he understood that for the settlers they were a symbol of labor and hope. There's a chill of superiority in contempt, and it isn't easy to admit to yourself. James wrote a short but famous essay, “On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings.” In it he says that we are almost always blind to the inner significance of other people's lives: what is full of meaning for someone else seems empty and absurd to us from the outside. Contempt is often exactly this kind of blindness. You don't need to overcome it right away. You can simply allow that you aren't seeing everything.
contempt.practice: About the person you feel contempt for, complete the sentence: “Perhaps this matters to them because…” One guess is enough — one clearing was enough for James.

disgust.text: We grimace, draw back, feel queasy — and only then, for James, do we “feel disgust”: the emotion is the perception of these bodily changes. It's a strong, ancient feeling, and there's no need to be ashamed of it. Disgust is above all the body saying “step away.” It's an ancient protective mechanism, and it fires faster than thought. So disgust toward a person, a situation or even yourself doesn't always mean a considered judgment: the body may be reacting to a smell, a tone, a memory. James suggested noticing how expressing a feeling intensifies it. If you soften your posture and breathing a little, it sometimes becomes visible what lies behind the disgust — fear, hurt, or simply tiredness.
disgust.practice: Notice how disgust shows up in your body: face, shoulders, stomach. Gently relax one place and see what changes.

revenge.text: Any thought that occupies consciousness, for James, tends by itself toward being carried out — he called this “ideo-motor action.” If you long for revenge, you've been hurt, and a force demanding justice is looking for an outlet; that doesn't make you a bad person. James would suggest looking at where your attention is pointed. Will, he believed, largely comes down to what we hold our attention on. Revenge fantasies don't mean you are “wicked”; they are a thought demanding an outlet and therefore taking up the whole field. You needn't fight it head-on — you can gently widen your attention: what else is true in this situation? What do you need right now — protection, recognition, peace?
revenge.practice: Say the revenge fantasy to yourself in one sentence, then finish out loud: “What I really need is…” — protection, recognition, peace. Attention moved to the need, for James, changes the action itself.

anger_at_loved.text: “We are mere walking bundles of habits,” James wrote — and we have the most habits with the people we live with. Anger at loved ones flares up in many of us, and so does the shame after it, but you are not a bad person because it arises. James wrote that habits are “grooves” in the nervous system: what is repeated begins to happen by itself, before we have time to think. We spend the most time with those close to us, so it is with them that the deepest grooves of reaction form — often dating back to childhood, or coming from tiredness. An outburst is not a verdict on your love but a well-worn path along which a nervous impulse ran. James believed grooves can be changed little by little: not through grand promises, but through small repeated actions, started at the first opportunity.
anger_at_loved.practice: Choose one tiny new gesture for moments of irritation — an exhale, a step to the side, the words “give me a minute” — and try it today. A groove begins to change with the first repetition.

ambivalence.text: Does a man running round a tree go round the squirrel that keeps hiding behind the trunk? James replied: both sides are right, depending on what you mean by “round.” Loving someone and being unable to stand them is a similar riddle. In The Varieties of Religious Experience James devoted a whole chapter to “the divided self”: he described people in whom opposing strivings coexist, and treated this with great sympathy. He also insisted on “pluralism”: reality doesn't have to reduce to a single formula, and experience can hold things that logically argue with each other. Mixed feelings toward someone close are neither a mistake nor a sign of falseness. They reflect the fact that relationships have many layers. James believed that inner unity comes gradually, sometimes on its own, and doesn't need to be forcibly hurried.
ambivalence.practice: Tell yourself: “Both are in me, and both feelings are true — depending on which side of the tree you look from.” Notice how your body responds.

guilty_relief.text: Consciousness, for James, sounds not as a single note but as a chord: in each moment, feelings that ought to exclude each other live side by side. If after a breakup, a departure or a loved one's long illness you feel relief along with sharp guilt, know this: relief doesn't cancel love but lives alongside it. James treated such mixed states with great sympathy. Relief and grief can flow side by side without pushing each other out. James, who himself knew long periods of exhaustion, also understood how costly prolonged strain is. When it ends, body and soul breathe out, and that is natural. Your relief speaks of how much you have endured.
guilty_relief.practice: Put your hand on your chest and say: “I feel relief, and I love.” Let both sentences sound together, like a chord.

indifference.text: The world can suddenly turn “flat,” alien and colorless — James collected such accounts in The Varieties of Religious Experience and knew the state from his own years of crisis. If where something “should” move you there is silence inside, it's frightening, but it doesn't make you heartless. Be gentle with yourself. He stressed that this isn't a person's choice: the sense that things matter is a gift that can temporarily weaken. James also taught that emotions are largely bodily. Indifference may simply be a sign of the organism's tiredness, not a moral flaw. You don't need to force yourself to feel the “right” way. James believed that the stream of consciousness changes, and colors have a way of coming back.
indifference.practice: Today, note one tiny thing that stirred even a shadow of response: a taste, a sound, warmth. Even a shadow counts — for James, colors come back little by little.

escape.text: “Moral holidays” — James wrote with sympathy about the need to let go, at least for a while, of the constant strain of responsibility. The wish to drop everything and leave says something important — about the freshness you're missing. James called habit “the enormous fly-wheel of society”: it keeps us in our groove, which both saves and constrains us. Over the years, he wrote, a person almost grows into their profession and manners. The dream of escape is a longing for rest from the groove and for unused powers: James believed we usually live on only part of our energy. You don't have to tear your life down. You can look into what kind of freshness you are missing.
escape.practice: Give yourself a fifteen-minute “moral holiday”: do something you never do in your usual role.

quote.text: Habit is thus the enormous fly-wheel of society, its most precious conservative agent.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. IV “Habit” (1890)

forbidden_attraction.text: Consciousness, James wrote, is a stream in which images and desires we never ordered keep surfacing. Attraction to someone who is “off-limits” can be embarrassing and frightening, but the feeling itself is not yet an act or a verdict. James described “the divided self”: a state in which different strivings live in a person at the same time, and one of them seems foreign to them. He wrote about it without moralizing, as a natural part of inner life. Attraction speaks rather of what your stream is looking for: novelty, attention, a different version of yourself. It's useful to ask what part of your life this feeling is telling you about. Understanding it doesn't commit you to anything.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Name silently, in one word, how you feel near this person. Then ask, like a pragmatist: where else in my life could this word be given room?

social_anxiety.text: “Whistling to keep up courage is no mere figure of speech,” James wrote. Shyness and fear of judgment are heavy and keep many people apart from others; James suggested going not against the feeling but through the body. James wrote that a person has as many “social selves” as there are people who know them: we are a little different with each. That's why another person's opinion touches us so sharply — it seems to create one of our selves. But James also offered a practical thought: feeling and action are more closely linked than it seems. We can't always order a feeling to vanish, but we can change our posture, voice and breathing a little — and the feeling follows. So you don't need to wait for the fear to pass. You can take a small step together with the fear.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a conversation, square your shoulders, lower them, take a slow exhale — and, if no one can hear, quietly whistle a few bars. Don't wait for the fear to disappear — just begin.

quote.text: Action seems to follow feeling, but really action and feeling go together.
quote.author: William James

uncertainty.text: In April 1906 an earthquake woke James at Stanford, and he later admitted feeling not fear but “glee and welcome,” as if saying to the earth, “Go it, and go it stronger!” Uncertainty is exhausting: the mind wants to know how everything will end, and knowing is impossible. He considered the universe “pluralistic” and unfinished: the future isn't written in advance; it holds real possibilities. This is unsettling, but for James it is also where our freedom lies: since the outcome isn't predetermined, our actions really do affect something. In the essay “Is Life Worth Living?” he wrote that life always involves risk, and that our faith in a possible result sometimes itself helps bring it about. Uncertainty is not only a threat but also a space in which your steps matter.
uncertainty.practice: Take a five-minute walk along a new route — turn where you've never been. James considered the world unfinished; notice what it's like to walk without knowing what's around the corner.

quote.text: It is only by risking our persons from one hour to another that we live at all.
quote.author: William James

waiting.text: An hour in a queue drags on forever and is forgotten at once, while a week of travel flies by yet looms large in memory — James noticed this paradox of time. When you're waiting for results, an answer or news, time stretches out agonizingly. It seems there's nothing to do but watch the clock. Moreover, he wrote that waiting itself fixes our attention on the passing of time. The agony of waiting is not your weakness but a law of perception. And a gentle piece of advice follows from it: fill the time you spend waiting a little. Not to forget, but so as not to leave yourself alone with an empty clock face.
waiting.practice: Fill the next hour with one activity for your hands or eyes — cooking, a walk, drawing. For James, filled time passes faster; see whether it does.

regret.text: If the world is a mechanism wound up in advance, regret makes no sense: so the determinist argued, and James answered him with a whole lecture, “The Dilemma of Determinism.” Regret that won't let go turns out, in it, to be surprisingly important evidence. He reasoned like this: if we regret something, we thereby admit that things could have been otherwise, that the world is not a mechanism written out in advance. Regret, for James, is evidence that people have real choice and that their actions carry weight. Your pain speaks of freedom and responsibility, not of worthlessness. But the same thought implies: since the future is open too, regret can be turned into an understanding of how you want to act from now on.
regret.practice: Picture the fork where you stood back then, and honestly live a minute of the other path in your imagination — without embellishment. Then ask: what does that path teach me for the next fork?

longing.text: James compared habits to grooves: we get used to a voice, to gestures, to shared rituals — and when the person isn't near, the grooves go on waiting for them. If you miss one particular person, it is a deep feeling, and there is nothing shameful in it. James would explain where it comes from. James wrote that our self is much wider than the body: it includes the people close to us, our home, everything we call “mine.” The loss or absence of someone close, in his words, is felt as the loss of a part of oneself. Longing is your extended self feeling an empty place. You don't have to hurry it. It shows how much this person has become part of you.
longing.practice: Today, carry out one of the habits you shared — the same walk, the same tea, the same song — as a sign of connection rather than a wound.

world_pain.text: Meliorism — James's name for the position between despair and carefree optimism: the world is neither doomed nor saved, and it can be made better. When hard news, violence and injustice hurt you, it's a sign that you are capable of compassion. James did not turn away from suffering: he wrote that the “sick soul,” which sees the evil in the world, may see reality more broadly than the cheerful optimist. But he didn't propose despair either. Every contribution, for James, matters. Your pain needs neither to be numbed nor grown without limit. It can be turned into a small contribution, proportionate to your strength. And don't forget to rest: meliorism is a long road, not a sprint.
world_pain.practice: Choose one concrete good deed for this week — a small melioristic contribution. Then allow yourself an hour without news.

rejection.text: A person, James wrote, has as many social selves as there are people and groups who know them — and each sees them in its own way. When you've been rejected — for a job, a friendship, a love — it wounds deeply, and James understood well why. He wrote about the “social self” — the recognition we get from others — and considered the need to be noticed one of the strongest in a human being. That's why rejection feels almost like physical pain. One person's rejection wounds one of these selves, but it doesn't cancel all the others. You can give yourself time to grieve — and remember those in whose eyes you still exist, matter and are loved.
rejection.practice: Call one of the people around whom you feel noticed — just to hear their voice. Let another of your selves answer.

quote.text: No more fiendish punishment could be devised, were such a thing physically possible, than that one should be turned loose in society and remain absolutely unnoticed by all the members thereof.
quote.author: William James
quote.source: The Principles of Psychology, ch. X (1890)

abandonment.text: “Do you like me or not?” — James took this question seriously in “The Will to Believe,” as a philosophical problem. If you're afraid of being left, it's a deep and painful feeling, and it deserves gentleness. The answer often depends on whether I myself am willing to take a step toward you, to believe it is possible. For James, there are truths that are created by trust: relationships hold together because each person acts in the faith that the other will also be there. The fear is understandable, since trust is always a risk. But it also suggests that you are not merely waiting passively to see whether you'll be left: your small steps of trust take part in creating the bond.
abandonment.practice: Today, make one small gesture of trust toward someone close — a message, a question, a thank-you — and notice what you feel as you do it.

unrequited.text: Jack is in love with Jill, and everyone around shrugs: what does he see in her? In “On a Certain Blindness in Human Beings,” James asked which of them is closer to the truth. If you love without being loved back, your pain is real, and James would be on the lover's side. James leaned toward the view that the lover sees what is really there, and the others are blind. Your love is not foolishness or a mistake but a special keenness of sight for another person's worth. Its going unanswered doesn't cancel this keenness. But it's important to turn the same ability to see worth toward yourself as well: you too deserve that kind of gaze.
unrequited.practice: Write down what you saw in this person — as keen-eyed as Jack. And beside it, one quality of your own that deserves the same gaze.

humiliation.text: “Self-feeling” — James's name for the primary emotions of self-satisfaction and self-dissatisfaction, which, he showed, depend strongly on the recognition of others. If you were humiliated in front of others, as if stripped of dignity, it is not your fault that this happened. It is one of the most painful experiences there is. Humiliation strikes exactly there: at the “social self,” at the image in which we are seen. But James stressed that we have many social selves, and that the core of the person — the stream of consciousness, the living sense of oneself from within — belongs to no one else's gaze. Humiliation wounds one facet of you but does not take away your self. You can give the wound time to heal.
humiliation.practice: Tell yourself: “What was done to me is not who I am.” Find a person around whom you feel your dignity.

body_shame.text: The body, James wrote, is the “innermost part” of our material self: we experience it as ourselves. That's why any judgment of the body wounds so deeply, and why dissatisfaction with it is so common and painful. And his formula of self-esteem — successes divided by pretensions — suggests where part of this pain comes from: from a huge “denominator,” from expectations that are often imposed from outside. James noted that giving up some pretensions is as much a relief as achieving them. You needn't fight your body; you can reconsider your demands on it. The body is not a project to be graded but the one that lets you live and feel.
body_shame.practice: Rest your palm on the part of your body you judge most often and tell it: “Today I give up this pretension.” James promised that giving up brings relief — notice whether it comes.

illness.text: A mountain climb in the Adirondacks in 1898 strained James's heart, and he lived his last twelve years with a damaged heart — writing The Varieties of Religious Experience and Pragmatism in that time. When your body lets you down, the ground slips away, and you have every right to be upset. James knew this firsthand: almost all his life he struggled with problems with his back, eyes and heart, and with long periods of exhaustion. In The Varieties of Religious Experience he wrote with respect about people who found meaning and support in the hardest circumstances. Illness is part of human experience, not a defeat. James proposed testing ideas by how they help us live. You might ask: what thought about your illness makes this day a little easier?
illness.practice: Find one sentence — from a book, a letter, a song — that makes today a little easier, and read it aloud. James tested ideas by how they help us live.

pride.text: James considered “self-complacency” a primary emotion, as natural and necessary as joy. Your pride in what you've done is a healthy and deserved feeling, and there's no need to hide it. James saw nothing shameful in it. He described how it shows in the body: upright posture, ease of movement, the urge to act. It is a signal from the organism: “you did it, you can.” And his formula of self-esteem — successes divided by pretensions — reminds us that the feeling of accomplishment doesn't have to be postponed until huge victories. If you've done what mattered to you, the “numerator” has grown. Let yourself enjoy this moment without comparing it to other people's successes.
pride.practice: Straighten up, take a deep breath and name out loud one thing you've done. Stay in that feeling for half a minute.

melancholy.text: No state, James wrote, ever returns exactly as it was: the stream of consciousness knows no repetitions. A quiet sadness, sorrow mixed with tenderness, is the feeling of that knowledge, and it doesn't need “fixing.” James distinguished two types of soul: the “healthy-minded,” which sees the world as bright, and the “sick soul,” which feels its fragility and shadow. For him the word “sick” was not a verdict. He believed that such a view may take in reality more broadly, because it doesn't turn away from loss, and that the deepest worldviews are born from contact with it. Your melancholy is not a breakdown but a special sensitivity to what passes. Perhaps gentle sadness is simply the knowledge that the stream never repeats.
melancholy.practice: Step outside or to a window for a couple of minutes and notice what, at this moment, is passing and will not come again.
